title: Why Your Furnace Short Cycles — Causes & Fixes
question: Why does my furnace keep turning on and off every few minutes?
summary: Furnace short cycling — turning on and off every few minutes instead of running full heating cycles — is most often caused by a dirty air filter or an overheating limit switch, but can also signal a thermostat, flame-sensor, or oversizing problem. Start with the filter; escalate to a licensed pro for anything involving the gas burner or repeated safety lockouts.

commonCauses.cause: Clogged or dirty air filter restricting airflow, causing the heat exchanger to overheat and trip the high-limit switch
commonCauses.quickCheck: Pull the filter and hold it up to a light — if you can't see light through it, it's too dirty. Check the date; most 1-inch filters need changing every 1-3 months.

commonCauses.cause: Overheating that trips the high-limit safety switch (from blocked airflow: dirty filter, closed/blocked supply or return vents, or a failing blower motor)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Walk the house and confirm supply registers and return grilles are open and unblocked by furniture or rugs. Listen for the blower — if the burner fires but little air moves, the blower may be failing.

commonCauses.cause: Dirty flame sensor — the burner lights, then shuts off after a few seconds because the sensor can't confirm flame
commonCauses.quickCheck: Watch the burners through the inspection window: if they ignite and then go out within a few seconds, repeatedly, a dirty or corroded flame sensor is the classic symptom.

commonCauses.cause: Thermostat problem — bad location (in a draft, near a vent, or in direct sun), low batteries, loose wiring, or a too-fast 'cycle rate' (digital stats) or mis-set heat anticipator (older mechanical stats)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Check that the thermostat isn't above a supply vent or in sunlight, replace its batteries, and confirm it reads a steady room temperature.

commonCauses.cause: Blocked or restricted flue / exhaust venting, or a failing pressure switch / induced-draft motor tripping the safety
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look outside for a blocked PVC exhaust/intake (snow, leaves, nest) on high-efficiency units. Listen for the small induced-draft motor running before ignition.

commonCauses.cause: Oversized furnace — too much capacity heats the space fast and satisfies the thermostat before a full cycle completes
commonCauses.quickCheck: If short cycling has happened since the unit was installed (not a new problem), and the filter/sensor are clean, oversizing is a likely culprit — needs a pro load calculation to confirm.

commonCauses.cause: Corroded or cracked heat exchanger, or a faulty high-limit switch itself
commonCauses.quickCheck: Repeated lockouts after the filter and flame sensor are clean point to a control or heat-exchanger issue — stop DIY and call a pro; a cracked heat exchanger is a carbon-monoxide hazard.

fixes: Replace the air filter with the correct size and a matching MERV rating (most systems do best with MERV 8-11; very high MERV can itself choke airflow). This alone fixes a large share of short-cycling cases.
Open every supply register and clear furniture, rugs, and boxes away from supply and return vents so the furnace can move air freely.

Set the thermostat to 'Heat,' replace its batteries, and make sure it isn't mounted in sun, a draft, or above a vent. On programmable models, set the cycle-rate/cycles-per-hour to the gas-furnace setting (usually the slowest, often labeled for gas or 'slow').

If the furnace reports a safety lockout or repeatedly stops after ignition, stop using it and call a licensed HVAC professional. Do not repeatedly reset it or open the burner compartment; the safety control is tripping for a reason.

A flame-sensor symptom (burners ignite and stop within seconds) requires professional combustion-system diagnosis and service; do not remove or clean components inside the burner compartment as a DIY step.
On high-efficiency units, check the outside PVC intake/exhaust pipes for snow, leaves, ice, or nests and clear any blockage.

If short cycling persists after a clean filter, open vents, thermostat checks, and a ground-level exterior vent check, stop using the furnace and call a licensed HVAC technician. Overheating, flame-sensor, pressure-switch, combustion, venting, or heat-exchanger issues require professional diagnosis.
diyVsPro: DIY is limited to replacing the correct filter, opening vents, replacing thermostat batteries, and checking a reachable exterior intake or exhaust from the ground. Do not open the burner compartment, manipulate gas controls, clean a flame sensor, or reset repeated lockouts. Use a licensed HVAC professional for every combustion, burner, flame-sensor, pressure-switch, venting, control, or heat-exchanger issue.
typicalCostUSD: Filter: $10-40. Thermostat batteries: ~$5. DIY flame-sensor cleaning: ~$0 (or a $15-25 replacement sensor). Pro service call/diagnostic: $80-200. Flame sensor replacement by a pro: $80-250. Pressure switch or limit switch: $150-400. Blower motor: $300-700. Control board: $300-600. Cracked heat exchanger usually means furnace replacement: $3,000-7,000+.
timeEstimate: Filter swap, opening vents, thermostat batteries: 5-15 minutes. Flame-sensor cleaning: 20-40 minutes. A pro diagnostic visit: 1-2 hours.
safetyNote: A short-cycling gas furnace may be overheating or shutting down for a combustion, venting, or heat-exchanger fault that can create fire or carbon-monoxide risk. Do not keep resetting it or open the burner compartment. If you smell gas or a CO alarm sounds, do not touch switches or equipment; evacuate immediately and call 911 or the gas utility from outside. Leave all internal furnace work to a licensed HVAC technician.
